opening: How is a probability-based system, like an AI model, different from a rules-based system?
closing: That's the end of today's review. Nice work thinking these through. You can press End conversation whenever you're ready.
note: Three short explain-in-your-own-words questions, asked in order. A good explanation moves on; a weak one gets discussion and hints (each hint is a concrete everyday scene, getting closer to the idea), never the answer.

questions.objective: Distinguish probabilistic AI behavior from deterministic UI/UX design.
questions.question: How is a probability-based system, like an AI model, different from a rules-based system?
questions.goodEnough: Explains that a rules-based system follows behavior people wrote in advance, so the same input gives the same output, while a probability-based system learns patterns from data and picks likely outputs, so results can vary.
lookFor: rules-based: behavior written by people, same input gives same output
probability-based: behavior learned from data, outputs can vary
errors in AI can come from data or context, not just code
designers shape AI behavior indirectly (prompts, data, examples)
hints: Picture a vending machine: you press B3 and get the same drink every time. Now picture asking a friend for advice. Which one works more like an AI model?
Someone set up the vending machine in advance. Where does your friend's advice come from instead?
If you asked that friend the same question on two different days, would you get exactly the same words?
misconceptions: different answers mean the AI is broken
AI is just a very large set of rules

questions.topic: What is a data-driven AI service?
questions.objective: Explain how data, models, interaction, service logic, evaluation, and governance work together.
questions.question: Besides the AI model itself, what other parts does an AI service need to work well?
questions.goodEnough: Names at least two non-model parts (data, interaction/interface, service logic, evaluation and governance) and briefly says what one of them does.
lookFor: data such as watch history or ratings
the interface where you see and react to it
service rules such as age ratings or not repeating
checking that it works and is fair, and protecting data
hints: Imagine Netflix with only the AI model and nothing else. What would it need to know about you first?
Where do you actually see the recommendation, and what can you click on?
What stops Netflix from recommending a horror movie to a 7-year-old, even if the model picked it?
How would Netflix find out whether its recommendations are actually good?
misconceptions: the model is the whole service

questions.topic: Integrating foundation models into interactive systems
questions.objective: Explain how existing foundation models are constrained and transformed for interactive services, including their opportunities and challenges.
questions.question: When we build a foundation model into an interactive service, what are some opportunities it opens up, and what challenges come with it?
questions.goodEnough: Gives at least one concrete opportunity and at least one concrete challenge from integrating foundation models into interactive systems, and briefly explains why each matters for users or designers.
lookFor: opportunities: natural-language or multimodal interaction, fast creation of content, flexible support for many goals, personalized help, mixed-initiative collaboration, tool use and automation, faster prototyping
challenges: hallucination or wrong answers, inconsistent behavior, hard to explain, bias, privacy and memory, overreliance on AI, hard to evaluate, unclear responsibility
a flexible general chatbot can leave users unsure what to ask or how to judge answers
the design question is what interaction to build around the model so it is useful, understandable and controllable
hints: Before AI, you clicked through menus to get things done. What changes when you can just say what you want in plain words?
What could happen if an AI gives a confident but wrong answer to someone who trusts it?
What if the AI remembers personal things you told it, or no one is sure who is responsible when it makes a mistake?
misconceptions: more capability always makes a better service
challenges will disappear once models get better
